newsitem.title: USA: Feds seeking source of Olympic bomb leak.
newsitem.headline: Feds seeking source of Olympic bomb leak.

text.p: The Justice Department is trying to identify the source of news leaks identifying Richard Jewell as a suspect in the Centennial Olympic Park bombing and will prosecute anyone found responsible, according to court documents filed on Thursday.

At a hearing before a federal judge this week, U.S. Attorney Kent Alexander said Attorney General Janet Reno and FBI director Louis Freeh had ordered an investigation into leaks surrounding the July 27 attack on the Summer Olympics.

Jewell became the only named suspect when the Atlanta Journal-Constitution identified him as the focus of the investigation days after a homemade pipebomb exploded in downtown Atlanta leaving two dead and more than 100 injured.
Other news organisations later claimed to have inside information on the case as well.

Federal officials have said they believe the information could have come from within the Justice Department or from other law enforcement agencies. A spokesman for the U.S. Attorney's Office in Atlanta declined to comment on the case.

"I have spoken personally with the attorney general (and) the director of the FBI about it. Their investigation is under way. If I find out who it is, I will gladly and vigorously prosecute them," Alexander told U.S. District Judge J. Owen Forrester according to transcripts.

The hearing was held on Tuesday on a Journal-Constitution request to examine sealed FBI documents contained in affidavits used to obtain search warrants against Jewell. Lawyers for the newspaper were present.

At the time of the attack, Jewell, 33, was a security guard at a nearby AT&T Corp. pavillion. Initially hailed as a hero for discovering the device and helping police clear crowds before it detonated, he was later identified as a suspect and was forced by the relentless glare of national media attention to live as a recluse for weeks as FBI agents camped outside his door, ready to follow his every move.

Jewell has since hired two lawyers who could sue the U.S. government and news media, including the Journal-Constitution. They say publicity surrounding the case had ruined the now unemployed security guard's chances of finding a job.

Alexander told the court the news leak was not part of an orchestrated effort by the FBI to identify Jewell as a suspect in the public eye. "Far from it," he said. "The media coverage relating to Mr. Jewell threw the investigation off course."

Jewell has never been charged with a crime and has steadfastly maintained his innocence. Earlier this week, his lawyers said federal officials had dropped their surveillance and agreed to issue a letter clearing his name if satisfied with his answers to a six-hour interrogation last Sunday.
